# Independent checkpoint review — Explore It!

Review the finished checkpoint from a fresh plain clone/export under /tmp, never another worktree. The authorized repository is /root/Software/booknotes-work/explore-it; do not touch /root/Software/book-notes or any other checkout. Scope only books/explore-it and scratch /tmp. No agents, no commits, no pushes, no unrelated service changes. Use Muse Wonder Full Standard mode.

Read AGENTS.md, books/explore-it/PLAN.md, register/BUILD-STATE.md and this checkpoint's records fully. The user specifically authorizes continued progress despite failed checks; report FAIL honestly and actionable repair, do not ask permission or stop later work. This is independent review, not an explorer; you may read answer-key register.

Check repo review bar and plan adaptation: baseline v0 functioning, historical black-box reproductions meaningful and failures distinguished from absence, current checks truly enforce named oracles, lesson pointers/citations and claims accurate, no fabricated dwell or scores, immutable explorer records and blind exports audited against machine transcript, single-purpose linear commits and tags correct. Raw report counts differ from reconciled catalogue fault counts; preserve the distinction. Recon found nearly the whole register early, legitimately shifting repairs into lesson 01; evaluate measured work rather than insisting on fictional later discoveries.

Use isolated Compose project names, images and ports if running checks, never reset shared active stack. Record exact commands/outcomes and budget or infrastructure limits. Return PASS/NITS/FAIL with file:line findings, material risks, and which checks you actually ran. Save report to specified /tmp report path. Do not alter SUT or write into original repository.

Checkpoint A target: b839fdf / explore-it/lesson-01. The fresh clone is /tmp/explore-it-review-a. Read book STATE.md first. Save your report /tmp/explore-it-coordinator/review-a.md. Use isolated current stack COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=queuelet-review-a QUEUELET_IMAGE_TAG=review-a QUEUELET_API_PORT=18260 QUEUELET_HOOK_PORT=18261 QUEUELET_PG_PORT=15493 QUEUELET_URL=http://localhost:18260 QUEUELET_HOOK_URL=http://localhost:18261. REF verifier owns queuelet-ref on18210/18211/15443; no other REF run is active. Do not touch explorer stacks. Current/historical35-case suites have real minute fixtures and current verification repeats cases as regression checks; allow their measured6.5-minute budget rather than demand the original two-finding estimate. Full source-text citations beyond publisher public excerpts were unavailable; assess the explicitly limited claims honestly.

Permission profile: local review scratch and isolated queuelet test operations, no source edits or git commits. At end stop your own review containers. Budget30minutes, prioritize material correctness and real independent checks over cosmetic findings. The active coordinator will retain your report and can repair findings in a fresh unit; no direct source changes.

1|# Explore It! — breakdown plan v2: one inherited job queue, learned through nine experiments
2|
3|**Book:** *Explore It! Reduce Risk and Increase Confidence with Exploratory Testing*, Elisabeth
4|Hendrickson, Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2013 (first edition, the only one; 186 pages, ISBN
5|978-1-937785-02-4). Chapter and section numbers below are from that edition's table of contents
6|(verified against the publisher's preview).
7|
8|**Phase:** plan (v2), for Nick's confirmation. Design only: no SUT code, no experiments, no skills
9|exist yet. Written on branch `plan/explore-it` in its own worktree while the Release It! build runs on
10|`main`; this pass adds files under `books/explore-it/` only. Suggested edits to `AGENTS.md`, the root
11|`README.md` and `STATE.md` are listed in section 10 as notes, to be applied when the branch merges.
12|
13|**What changed from v1.** Nick scoped the book: *"That book had a lot of fluff so feel free to skip
14|shallow concepts or netting with people soft skills things. I'm interested in the probing, testing,
15|learning of new codebase part."* And the shape he wants: *"a good system in place with interesting
16|experiments set of to learn about it and cool skills to explore codebases."* v2 is v1 cut to that
17|centre. Section 0 says what was cut and why what remains is the book's core. The vehicle is unchanged.
18|Eleven lessons became **nine experiments**; eight people-and-process skills became **eight
19|codebase-exploration skills** (different eight); the register gained one defect and lost one lesson's
20|worth of theatre. The v1 → v2 changelog is at the end.
21|
22|---
23|
24|## 0. What this plan deliberately omits, and why the rest is the book's real core
25|
26|Hendrickson's book has two layers. One is a **method for learning a system you did not write by
27|experimenting on it**: state what you think it does, poke it in a way that would prove you wrong,
28|watch everything it reveals (not just the response), and fold what you learned into a model that
29|tells you where to poke next. That layer is Chapters 2–9 and the parts of 10–13 that are about the
30|system. The other layer is about **people and teams**: how to talk to stakeholders, pair, estimate,
31|run requirements meetings, debrief managers and build a team's heuristics list. Nick asked for the
32|first layer only. This plan takes him at his word.
33|
34|| Omitted | Book sections | What v1 had for it | Why it goes |
35||---|---|---|---|
36|| Stakeholder interviews and "sharing observations" | 11.2, 11.3 | a written Q&A with the coordinator playing product owner in L01 | theatre about communication; the questions it produced come just as well from reading the spec and the code (12.4, folded into E01) |
37|| Requirements meetings and chartering during them | 12.1, 12.2, 12.3 | L10, a whole lesson with "decisions.md" from a role-played product owner | a meeting technique; the one durable idea (the spec is silent, so the code decided: find out what) is now a hypothesis source in every experiment, and the four planted ambiguities are re-homed in the experiments that probe them |
38|| Personas | 6.3 | the maintenance operator, the impatient producer, the flaky worker in L05 | a shallow generator; the sequences it produced come from nouns × verbs and the state table directly |
39|| Paired exploration, estimating, "explored enough", stakeholder debriefs, the team's nuggets list, exploration in the test strategy | 13.1, 13.2, 13.4, 13.5, 13.6, 13.7 | L11, a 90-minute paired session with `STRATEGY.md` and a debrief written for Nick | team process; the one systemic idea in Ch. 13 (13.3, read the defect list for causes) is now the last experiment, E09, and "findings become regression checks" is the fixer's standing rule rather than a strategy document |
40|| The Nightmare Headline Game as a group activity | 2.5 | the risk-brainstorm ritual closing the recon | the output (risk hypotheses) is kept as one of the hypothesis sources in `charter-as-probe`; the game is not |
41|| Practice sessions; interviewing testers; web heuristics; exploring a programming language | 1.4, A1, A2.2, 10.2 | omitted in v1 too | out of scope for an API-only SUT and a reader who is an engineer, not a hiring manager |

45|observing everything the system reveals and adding hooks when it reveals too little (Ch. 3), varying
46|inputs, data, state and sequences on purpose (Ch. 4, 6), knowing what "wrong" means when nobody wrote
47|it down (Ch. 5), building models (entities, states, ecosystem) whose empty cells are the next probes
48|(Ch. 7–9), doing it through tools because there is no UI (Ch. 10), starting with a recon of a system
49|you inherited (11.1, 11.4), characterizing a surprise down to its variables (10.4, 11.5–11.6), and
50|reading the defect list for what it says about how the code was written (13.3). That is the method,
51|and it is what an engineer dropped into a new codebase actually uses. The step count fell from eleven

55|## 1. The shape: experiments against an inherited codebase
56|
57|`AGENTS.md` was written for *Release It!*: the book names flaws in a system, so the archetype is a
58|flawed system and each lesson is a patch that fixes a flaw, with a verify script that reproduces the
59|flaw on the previous tag. *Explore It!* names no flaws in systems; it teaches a way of finding them.
60|The thing that gets better step by step is the **explorer's model of the system**, and the system
61|improves as a consequence. The adaptation keeps every structural element of the playbook and
62|changes what each one holds:
63|
64|| Playbook element | Release It! | Explore It! (this plan) |
65||---|---|---|
66|| The archetype | one flawed service, improved by patches | one **inherited** service (the system under test, SUT) seeded with realistic defects, plus the **exploration record** beside it (`exploration/`: hypotheses, probe logs, models, defect reports) |
67|| What a lesson is | one technique of the book applied as a fix | one **experiment**: a hypothesis about the system, a technique of the book used as the probe, a time-boxed run against the SUT, what the system revealed, how the model changed; then the defects it found are **fixed and turned into checks** |
68|| The lesson commit | patch + note + verify script | **two commits**: the experiment (charter, probe log, revealed, models, defect reports) and the fix (SUT patch + regression checks + note); the lesson tag points at the fix |
69|| The register | flaws → chapter → lesson | defects → **the probe that reveals them** → chapter → experiment; plus four spec silences (where the code decided) and three testability gaps |
70|| The verify | load + chaos + thresholds; `IMPROVED:` / `FLAW REPRODUCED:` | the experiment's black-box **reproduction scripts** plus the regression checks; `FIXED AND CHECKED:` / `DEFECTS REPRODUCED:`. `REF=<earlier tag>` shows the defect was present all along: the **dwell table** (which tags the defect sat in while earlier experiments ran past it) is the payoff |
71|| "Skill compounding" in `git log` | the system hardens | early experiments reveal shallow defects; later, better-modelled ones reveal the deep ones (stale acks, lost cancels, DST drift, a loop that silently dies) that the earlier ones walked past, and the last experiment predicts a defect from the pattern before probing for it |
72|| Skills | written after the lessons, from the lessons | written **before** the experiments, from the book, and **executed** by them; each experiment is a skill's worked example and sends corrections back |
73|
74|Three rules keep the record honest rather than theatre:
75|
76|1. **The explorer is blind to the register, not to the code.** The agent that runs an experiment
77|   never sees this plan's register, the proof scripts or the SUT's git history. It works from a
78|   plain export of the SUT tree (source included), the exploration record so far, the skill for the
79|   experiment and its charter. It **may read the code**: this is a book about learning a codebase,
80|   and reading is one of the two ways to form a hypothesis (the other is the running system). Every
81|   hypothesis records its source (spec, code, model, or a surprise) and whether the probe confirmed
82|   it. Defects it finds are real finds; defects it misses are recorded as misses and disclosed in the
83|   lesson note. The seeder (who plants the register) and the explorer are agents from **different
84|   model families**, which the repo's cross-family rule already requires for review.
85|2. **The record is committed as produced.** Probe logs keep their timestamps and their dead ends.
86|   The coordinator formats, never rewrites. A reader should be able to see an experiment go wrong.
87|3. **Every experiment is scored.** `revealed.md` ends with a table: hypotheses stated, confirmed,
88|   refuted; predictions made from reading the code that the running system contradicted; defects
89|   found; model cells filled. The score is the learning curve the lesson notes draw.
90|
91|Everything else in `AGENTS.md` (one archetype, real technology, `make up / make verify LESSON=NN
92|[REF=tag]`, lesson notes outside `project/`, tags, the review bar, commit style) applies unchanged.
93|"Lesson NN" in the repo's vocabulary is "experiment NN" in this plan's; they are the same thing.
94|
95|## 2. The book's core, as this plan uses it
96|
97|### 2.1 Core argument
98|
99|Testing is two activities. **Checking** confirms the software does what you already decided it
100|should; it is designed in advance and is what test cases and automated suites hold. **Exploring** is
101|designing experiments, running them and learning from the result in the same motion, so each
102|observation shapes the next experiment (Ch. 1.1, 1.2). Checks catch regressions in the risks you
103|named; exploration finds the risks you did not name. For an engineer inheriting a codebase the second
104|activity is the only one available on day one: there is nothing to check against yet, only a system
105|to learn. The book's program, stripped to that use: give each probe a **charter** so it has a
106|hypothesis and a budget (Ch. 2); **observe** what is actually happening, including what the interface
107|hides, and ask for hooks when it hides too much (Ch. 3); find the **variables** and vary them on
108|purpose (Ch. 4); decide what "wrong" means when no one wrote it down (Ch. 5); use **models** of
109|sequences, entities, states and the surrounding ecosystem as generators of probes (Ch. 6–9); do it
110|all through tools, because there is no UI (Ch. 10); start with a recon of the system you inherited
111|(11.1, 11.4); characterize every surprise to its minimal reproduction (10.4, 11.5–11.6); and read the
112|defect list for what it says about how the code was written (13.3).
113|
114|### 2.2 Chapter map (kept sections only)
115|
116|| Chapter | Sections kept | What it gives the explorer of a new codebase |
117||---|---|---|
118|| 1. On Testing and Exploration | 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 (the time box as a budget) | exploration as simultaneous learning, design and execution; the experiment as the unit |
119|| 2. Charter Your Explorations | 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6 (2.5 as a one-line hypothesis source) | the template *Explore `<target>` with `<resources>` to discover `<information>`*, read here as a hypothesis with instruments; too broad / too narrow; where hypotheses come from; a backlog of them |
120|| 3. Observe the Details | 3.1–3.4 | inattentional blindness; looking past the interface; asking for testability hooks; reading the consoles the system already has |
121|| 4. Find Interesting Variations | 4.1–4.4 | variables beyond input fields: counts, sizes, positions, timing, sequences, configuration; the named heuristics of A2.1 |
122|| 5. Evaluate Results | 5.1–5.3 | oracles when there is no spec: Never/Always rules, comparable systems and standards, approximations |
123|| 6. Vary Sequences and Interactions | 6.1, 6.2 | nouns and verbs combined in odd orders; random walks |
124|| 7. Explore Entities and Their Relationships | 7.1–7.3 | the entity model as a generator: entity × CRUD, dependency × "what happens to the dependent", data followed through every place it appears |
125|| 8. Discover States and Transitions | 8.1–8.4 | the state model as a generator: every state × every event, especially the cells the diagram has no arrow for |
126|| 9. Explore the Ecosystem | 9.1–9.4 | the context diagram; what crosses a trust boundary unchecked; "what if this neighbour misbehaves"; data across the boundary |
127|| 10. Explore When There Is No User Interface | 10.1, 10.3, 10.4 | tools as the interface; isolating a surprise to its minimal reproduction and the variables that matter |
128|| 11. Explore an Existing System | 11.1, 11.4, 11.5, 11.6 | the recon of an inherited system; which probe fits which question; recording findings; unreproducible bugs |
129|| 12. Explore Requirements | 12.4 only (active reading), folded into E01 and the hypothesis sources | reading a spec adversarially: what does it not say, what would make it false |
130|| 13. Integrate Exploration Throughout | 13.3 only | reading the defect list for causes, not symptoms |
131|| A2. Test Heuristics Cheat Sheet | A2.1 | the kit `sweep-variables` draws from |
132|
133|### 2.3 What an engineer does differently after this arc
134|
135|- Meets a new codebase with a **recon**: entry points, nouns and verbs, what the spec is silent on,
136|  what the code decided there, and a backlog of hypotheses ranked by what would hurt most.
137|- Writes each probe as a **charter with a hypothesis** and a budget, not as "poke around".
138|- Treats every observation as data: reads logs, the database and event histories alongside the
139|  response, and **adds hooks** (structured events, a controllable clock) when the system hides what
140|  it is doing.
141|- Names the **variables** of a surface before touching it and varies them with named heuristics
142|  instead of trying "a few values".
143|- Writes the **oracle** down before judging an output: the Never/Always rule, the comparable system,
144|  the approximation.
145|- Draws **models** (nouns and verbs, entities and CRUD, states and events, the ecosystem with its
146|  trust boundaries) because the model's blank cells are where the bugs are, and keeps them as living
147|  files.
148|- **Follows surprises** to a minimal reproduction with the variables isolated, then looks for the
149|  sibling: the same cause elsewhere in the code.
150|- Reads the defect list for **how the code was written** (a missing guard pattern, a silent-accept
151|  habit) and fixes the cause structurally, with a model-based check that keeps it fixed.
152|
153|The vocabulary is Hendrickson's (charters, sessions, heuristics, models). "Tours" are Whittaker's
154|(*Exploratory Software Testing*, 2009) and are not used.

156|## 3. The vehicle: `queuelet`, an inherited baby job queue, and the exploration record beside it
157|
158|### 3.0 Why this vehicle (unchanged from v1)
159|
160|What this arc needs is a system with **many states and events** (Ch. 8), **entities with
161|dependencies** (Ch. 7), **many nouns and verbs** that combine (Ch. 6), **variables of every kind**
162|including time (Ch. 4), an **ecosystem with a trust boundary** (Ch. 9), **no UI** (Ch. 10), a spec
163|that is silent in places (12.4) and a codebase small enough to read in an afternoon yet large enough
164|that reading alone does not reveal everything. Seeded defects must be **semantic** (wrong state, lost
165|cancel, off-by-one, precision loss, wrong timezone), the kind an engineer finds by thinking and
166|probing, not by load.
167|
168|| Candidate | Fit | Why it did or did not win |
169||---|---|---|
170|| **Reuse `litefleet`** (the Release It! SUT) | medium | Real, in Nick's domain, already built. But its register is stability-shaped (load and fault injection find its flaws), its tenant surface is a SQL passthrough with few verbs and little state of its own, and seeding it would mean editing the Release It! codebase during that arc. Litefleet stays a **second worked example** for two skills once both arcs land (section 7). |
171|| **A baby durable job queue** | near 1:1 | Nick's second domain. A job has eight states and a dozen events, so sneak paths are everywhere. Entities with real dependencies: queues own jobs and schedules, workers hold leases, schedules enqueue jobs. Verbs galore. Variables of every kind: payload size and numeric precision, priority, delay, batch count, cron with time zones. An ecosystem: Postgres, workers, a webhook partner across a trust boundary, the clock. No UI: an HTTP API and a CLI. A queue is the substrate of the workflow platform and of a deploy pipeline, so it is the smallest thing that still looks like what Nick builds. |
172|| Workflow platform | good but large | Everything fits, but the minimum (definitions, steps, timers, history) is 2–3× the budget before a single defect is planted; the queue is its kernel. |
173|| Baby Vercel product (deployments) | medium | Deployments have states, but a build pipeline needs real work to run and most of the richness is cost without exploration payoff. A deploy queue is, again, a job queue. |
174|
175|### 3.1 What it does
176|
177|`queuelet` is a single-binary job queue service over Postgres, the kind a small platform team writes
178|for itself and later wishes it had tested. Producers **enqueue** jobs (a kind, a JSON payload, a
179|priority, an optional delay) into named **queues** inside a **namespace** (the tenant). **Workers**
180|register, **lease** batches of jobs with a lease timeout, **heartbeat** to extend, and **ack** or
181|**nack** (with or without retry). The service **expires** leases of crashed workers, **retries** failed
182|jobs with backoff up to `max_attempts`, **dead-letters** the rest, fires **schedules** (cron
183|expressions in an IANA time zone), **purges** terminal jobs after a retention window, and **notifies** a
184|per-queue **webhook** (HMAC-signed) when a job reaches a terminal state. Operators pause, resume and
185|purge queues, cancel and retry jobs, and read stats. There is a CLI, `qctl`, for all of it. The
186|service is "inherited": it has a spec, thin tests, a README, and nobody on the team has explored it.
187|It is about 2 500 lines of Go: readable in an afternoon, which is the point.
188|
189|### 3.2 API (v0)
190|
191|All routes take `Authorization: Bearer <key>`; a key belongs to one namespace. One admin key sees
192|every namespace. Errors are `{"error": {"code", "message"}}` with 4xx/5xx status (with the exceptions
193|the register plants). Host port 18200.
194|
195|| Route | Purpose |
196||---|---|
197|| `POST /v1/queues` `{name, lease_seconds=30, max_attempts=3, backoff:{kind: exponential\|linear, base_seconds=5, max_seconds?}, retention_hours=24, webhook:{url, secret}?}` | create a queue |
198|| `GET /v1/queues`, `GET /v1/queues/{q}`, `PATCH /v1/queues/{q}`, `DELETE /v1/queues/{q}` | CRUD |
199|| `POST /v1/queues/{q}/pause`, `/resume`, `/purge` | operator verbs |
200|| `POST /v1/queues/{q}/jobs` `{kind, payload, priority=5 (0–9), run_at? \| delay_seconds?, max_attempts?, idempotency_key?}` → `201 {id, state}` | enqueue |
201|| `POST /v1/queues/{q}/jobs:batch` `{jobs:[…]}` (1–500) → `201 {ids}` | batch enqueue |
202|| `GET /v1/queues/{q}/jobs?state=&kind=&limit=&cursor=` | list (keyset paging) |
203|| `GET /v1/jobs/{id}`, `GET /v1/jobs/{id}/attempts`, `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/cancel`, `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/retry`, `DELETE /v1/jobs/{id}` | job verbs |
204|| `POST /v1/workers` `{name, kinds}` → `{worker_id, token}`; `DELETE /v1/workers/{id}` (releases its leases) | worker registry |
205|| `POST /v1/queues/{q}/lease` `{worker_id, max_jobs (1–100)}` → `{jobs:[{id, kind, payload, attempt, lease_token, lease_expires_at}]}` | lease a batch (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`) |
206|| `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/heartbeat` `{lease_token, extend_seconds}`; `/ack` `{lease_token, result}`; `/nack` `{lease_token, error, retry=true, delay_seconds?}` | the worker protocol |
207|| `POST /v1/schedules` `{name, queue, kind, payload, cron, timezone, enabled}`; `GET/PATCH/DELETE /v1/schedules/{id}`; `POST /v1/schedules/{id}/run` | cron schedules |
208|| `GET /v1/queues/{q}/stats`, `GET /v1/namespaces/{ns}/stats` | counts by state, oldest queued age, throughput |
209|| `GET /health`, `GET /metrics` (minimal) | ops |

211|Job states: `scheduled` (run_at in the future) → `queued` → `leased` → `succeeded` | `retry_wait` →
212|`queued` … | `dead`; `cancelled` from any non-terminal state. Events: enqueue, run_at reached,
213|lease, heartbeat, ack, nack(retry), nack(no retry), lease expired, cancel, retry, delete, purge,
214|retention sweep, worker deregistered, queue paused/resumed/deleted. The v0 code has no central
215|transition table; each handler's `UPDATE … WHERE` carries whatever guard its author remembered. That
216|is the pattern E09 names and fixes (Ch. 13.3).
217|
218|A background loop in the service, once per second: promote `scheduled` → `queued`; expire leases;
219|fire due schedules; sweep retention; ship the webhook outbox.
220|
221|**CLI** `qctl` (`queue create|ls|get|pause|resume|purge|rm`, `enqueue`, `jobs ls`, `job get|attempts|
222|cancel|retry|rm`, `worker run <q> --kinds …` (the sample worker), `schedule …`, `stats`; from E02
223|also `watch`, `job events` and `clock`). It is the explorer's main instrument (Ch. 10.1, 10.3), and
224|also its blind spot: it only ever sends well-formed requests (E03).

372|(Part II). Ch. 10 is practised in every experiment, since the SUT has no UI, and 10.4
373|(characterizing) is a rule of the protocol rather than a step. Last, the one Ch. 13 idea that is about
374|the code: read the findings for the pattern, predict from it, probe the prediction, fix the cause.
375|
376|**The leaner arc in one line:** *map it → make it visible → vary it → judge it → sequence it → relate
377|it → state it → surround it → explain it.* Each verb is one experiment and one probe family.

386|   surprise) and *I would be wrong if …* (what observation refutes it). One target, named
387|   instruments (tools, data, hooks, models, the spec, the source), one kind of information. The
388|   experiment's charter is written by the coordinator from this plan; the explorer may add
389|   hypotheses to the backlog, never widen the one it holds.

13|**What changed from v1.** Nick scoped the book: *"That book had a lot of fluff so feel free to skip
14|shallow concepts or netting with people soft skills things. I'm interested in the probing, testing,
15|learning of new codebase part."* And the shape he wants: *"a good system in place with interesting

17|centre. Section 0 says what was cut and why what remains is the book's core. The vehicle is unchanged.

23|
24|## 0. What this plan deliberately omits, and why the rest is the book's real core
25|
26|Hendrickson's book has two layers. One is a **method for learning a system you did not write by
27|experimenting on it**: state what you think it does, poke it in a way that would prove you wrong,
28|watch everything it reveals (not just the response), and fold what you learned into a model that
29|tells you where to poke next. That layer is Chapters 2–9 and the parts of 10–13 that are about the
30|system. The other layer is about **people and teams**: how to talk to stakeholders, pair, estimate,
31|run requirements meetings, debrief managers and build a team's heuristics list. Nick asked for the
32|first layer only. This plan takes him at his word.
33|
34|| Omitted | Book sections | What v1 had for it | Why it goes |
35||---|---|---|---|
36|| Stakeholder interviews and "sharing observations" | 11.2, 11.3 | a written Q&A with the coordinator playing product owner in L01 | theatre about communication; the questions it produced come just as well from reading the spec and the code (12.4, folded into E01) |

45|observing everything the system reveals and adding hooks when it reveals too little (Ch. 3), varying

55|## 1. The shape: experiments against an inherited codebase
56|
57|`AGENTS.md` was written for *Release It!*: the book names flaws in a system, so the archetype is a
58|flawed system and each lesson is a patch that fixes a flaw, with a verify script that reproduces the
59|flaw on the previous tag. *Explore It!* names no flaws in systems; it teaches a way of finding them.
60|The thing that gets better step by step is the **explorer's model of the system**, and the system
61|improves as a consequence. The adaptation keeps every structural element of the playbook and
62|changes what each one holds:
63|

65||---|---|---|

70|| The verify | load + chaos + thresholds; `IMPROVED:` / `FLAW REPRODUCED:` | the experiment's black-box **reproduction scripts** plus the regression checks; `FIXED AND CHECKED:` / `DEFECTS REPRODUCED:`. `REF=<earlier tag>` shows the defect was present all along: the **dwell table** (which tags the defect sat in while earlier experiments ran past it) is the payoff |
71|| "Skill compounding" in `git log` | the system hardens | early experiments reveal shallow defects; later, better-modelled ones reveal the deep ones (stale acks, lost cancels, DST drift, a loop that silently dies) that the earlier ones walked past, and the last experiment predicts a defect from the pattern before probing for it |
72|| Skills | written after the lessons, from the lessons | written **before** the experiments, from the book, and **executed** by them; each experiment is a skill's worked example and sends corrections back |

74|Three rules keep the record honest rather than theatre:
75|
76|1. **The explorer is blind to the register, not to the code.** The agent that runs an experiment
77|   never sees this plan's register, the proof scripts or the SUT's git history. It works from a
78|   plain export of the SUT tree (source included), the exploration record so far, the skill for the
79|   experiment and its charter. It **may read the code**: this is a book about learning a codebase,
80|   and reading is one of the two ways to form a hypothesis (the other is the running system). Every
81|   hypothesis records its source (spec, code, model, or a surprise) and whether the probe confirmed
82|   it. Defects it finds are real finds; defects it misses are recorded as misses and disclosed in the
83|   lesson note. The seeder (who plants the register) and the explorer are agents from **different
84|   model families**, which the repo's cross-family rule already requires for review.
85|2. **The record is committed as produced.** Probe logs keep their timestamps and their dead ends.
86|   The coordinator formats, never rewrites. A reader should be able to see an experiment go wrong.
87|3. **Every experiment is scored.** `revealed.md` ends with a table: hypotheses stated, confirmed,
88|   refuted; predictions made from reading the code that the running system contradicted; defects
89|   found; model cells filled. The score is the learning curve the lesson notes draw.
90|
91|Everything else in `AGENTS.md` (one archetype, real technology, `make up / make verify LESSON=NN
92|[REF=tag]`, lesson notes outside `project/`, tags, the review bar, commit style) applies unchanged.
93|"Lesson NN" in the repo's vocabulary is "experiment NN" in this plan's; they are the same thing.

95|## 2. The book's core, as this plan uses it
96|
97|### 2.1 Core argument
98|
99|Testing is two activities. **Checking** confirms the software does what you already decided it
100|should; it is designed in advance and is what test cases and automated suites hold. **Exploring** is
101|designing experiments, running them and learning from the result in the same motion, so each
102|observation shapes the next experiment (Ch. 1.1, 1.2). Checks catch regressions in the risks you
103|named; exploration finds the risks you did not name. For an engineer inheriting a codebase the second
104|activity is the only one available on day one: there is nothing to check against yet, only a system
105|to learn. The book's program, stripped to that use: give each probe a **charter** so it has a
106|hypothesis and a budget (Ch. 2); **observe** what is actually happening, including what the interface
107|hides, and ask for hooks when it hides too much (Ch. 3); find the **variables** and vary them on
108|purpose (Ch. 4); decide what "wrong" means when no one wrote it down (Ch. 5); use **models** of
109|sequences, entities, states and the surrounding ecosystem as generators of probes (Ch. 6–9); do it
110|all through tools, because there is no UI (Ch. 10); start with a recon of the system you inherited
111|(11.1, 11.4); characterize every surprise to its minimal reproduction (10.4, 11.5–11.6); and read the
112|defect list for what it says about how the code was written (13.3).
113|
114|### 2.2 Chapter map (kept sections only)
115|
116|| Chapter | Sections kept | What it gives the explorer of a new codebase |
117||---|---|---|
118|| 1. On Testing and Exploration | 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 (the time box as a budget) | exploration as simultaneous learning, design and execution; the experiment as the unit |
119|| 2. Charter Your Explorations | 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6 (2.5 as a one-line hypothesis source) | the template *Explore `<target>` with `<resources>` to discover `<information>`*, read here as a hypothesis with instruments; too broad / too narrow; where hypotheses come from; a backlog of them |
120|| 3. Observe the Details | 3.1–3.4 | inattentional blindness; looking past the interface; asking for testability hooks; reading the consoles the system already has |
121|| 4. Find Interesting Variations | 4.1–4.4 | variables beyond input fields: counts, sizes, positions, timing, sequences, configuration; the named heuristics of A2.1 |
122|| 5. Evaluate Results | 5.1–5.3 | oracles when there is no spec: Never/Always rules, comparable systems and standards, approximations |
123|| 6. Vary Sequences and Interactions | 6.1, 6.2 | nouns and verbs combined in odd orders; random walks |
124|| 7. Explore Entities and Their Relationships | 7.1–7.3 | the entity model as a generator: entity × CRUD, dependency × "what happens to the dependent", data followed through every place it appears |
125|| 8. Discover States and Transitions | 8.1–8.4 | the state model as a generator: every state × every event, especially the cells the diagram has no arrow for |
126|| 9. Explore the Ecosystem | 9.1–9.4 | the context diagram; what crosses a trust boundary unchecked; "what if this neighbour misbehaves"; data across the boundary |
127|| 10. Explore When There Is No User Interface | 10.1, 10.3, 10.4 | tools as the interface; isolating a surprise to its minimal reproduction and the variables that matter |

132|
133|### 2.3 What an engineer does differently after this arc
134|
135|- Meets a new codebase with a **recon**: entry points, nouns and verbs, what the spec is silent on,
136|  what the code decided there, and a backlog of hypotheses ranked by what would hurt most.
137|- Writes each probe as a **charter with a hypothesis** and a budget, not as "poke around".
138|- Treats every observation as data: reads logs, the database and event histories alongside the
139|  response, and **adds hooks** (structured events, a controllable clock) when the system hides what
140|  it is doing.
141|- Names the **variables** of a surface before touching it and varies them with named heuristics
142|  instead of trying "a few values".
143|- Writes the **oracle** down before judging an output: the Never/Always rule, the comparable system,
144|  the approximation.
145|- Draws **models** (nouns and verbs, entities and CRUD, states and events, the ecosystem with its
146|  trust boundaries) because the model's blank cells are where the bugs are, and keeps them as living
147|  files.
148|- **Follows surprises** to a minimal reproduction with the variables isolated, then looks for the
149|  sibling: the same cause elsewhere in the code.
150|- Reads the defect list for **how the code was written** (a missing guard pattern, a silent-accept
151|  habit) and fixes the cause structurally, with a model-based check that keeps it fixed.
152|
153|The vocabulary is Hendrickson's (charters, sessions, heuristics, models). "Tours" are Whittaker's
154|(*Exploratory Software Testing*, 2009) and are not used.

156|## 3. The vehicle: `queuelet`, an inherited baby job queue, and the exploration record beside it
157|
158|### 3.0 Why this vehicle (unchanged from v1)
159|
160|What this arc needs is a system with **many states and events** (Ch. 8), **entities with
161|dependencies** (Ch. 7), **many nouns and verbs** that combine (Ch. 6), **variables of every kind**
162|including time (Ch. 4), an **ecosystem with a trust boundary** (Ch. 9), **no UI** (Ch. 10), a spec
163|that is silent in places (12.4) and a codebase small enough to read in an afternoon yet large enough
164|that reading alone does not reveal everything. Seeded defects must be **semantic** (wrong state, lost
165|cancel, off-by-one, precision loss, wrong timezone), the kind an engineer finds by thinking and
166|probing, not by load.
167|
168|| Candidate | Fit | Why it did or did not win |
169||---|---|---|
170|| **Reuse `litefleet`** (the Release It! SUT) | medium | Real, in Nick's domain, already built. But its register is stability-shaped (load and fault injection find its flaws), its tenant surface is a SQL passthrough with few verbs and little state of its own, and seeding it would mean editing the Release It! codebase during that arc. No UI: an HTTP API and a CLI. A queue is the substrate of the workflow platform and of a deploy pipeline, so it is the smallest thing that still looks like what Nick builds. |
172|| Workflow platform | good but large | Everything fits, but the minimum (definitions, steps, timers, history) is 2–3× the budget before a single defect is planted; the queue is its kernel. |
173|| Baby Vercel product (deployments) | medium | Deployments have states, but a build pipeline needs real work to run and most of the richness is cost without exploration payoff. A deploy queue is, again, a job queue. |
174|
175|### 3.1 What it does
176|
177|`queuelet` is a single-binary job queue service over Postgres, the kind a small platform team writes
178|for itself and later wishes it had tested. Producers **enqueue** jobs (a kind, a JSON payload, a
179|priority, an optional delay) into named **queues** inside a **namespace** (the tenant). **Workers**
180|register, **lease** batches of jobs with a lease timeout, **heartbeat** to extend, and **ack** or
181|**nack** (with or without retry). The service **expires** leases of crashed workers, **retries** failed
182|jobs with backoff up to `max_attempts`, **dead-letters** the rest, fires **schedules** (cron
183|expressions in an IANA time zone), **purges** terminal jobs after a retention window, and **notifies** a
184|per-queue **webhook** (HMAC-signed) when a job reaches a terminal state. Operators pause, resume and
185|purge queues, cancel and retry jobs, and read stats. There is a CLI, `qctl`, for all of it. The
186|service is "inherited": it has a spec, thin tests, a README, and nobody on the team has explored it.
187|It is about 2 500 lines of Go: readable in an afternoon, which is the point.
188|
189|### 3.2 API (v0)
190|
191|All routes take `Authorization: Bearer <key>`; a key belongs to one namespace. One admin key sees
192|every namespace. Errors are `{"error": {"code", "message"}}` with 4xx/5xx status (with the exceptions
193|the register plants). Host port 18200.
194|
195|| Route | Purpose |
196||---|---|
197|| `POST /v1/queues` `{name, lease_seconds=30, max_attempts=3, backoff:{kind: exponential\|linear, base_seconds=5, max_seconds?}, retention_hours=24, webhook:{url, secret}?}` | create a queue |
198|| `GET /v1/queues`, `GET /v1/queues/{q}`, `PATCH /v1/queues/{q}`, `DELETE /v1/queues/{q}` | CRUD |
199|| `POST /v1/queues/{q}/pause`, `/resume`, `/purge` | operator verbs |
200|| `POST /v1/queues/{q}/jobs` `{kind, payload, priority=5 (0–9), run_at? \| delay_seconds?, max_attempts?, idempotency_key?}` → `201 {id, state}` | enqueue |
201|| `POST /v1/queues/{q}/jobs:batch` `{jobs:[…]}` (1–500) → `201 {ids}` | batch enqueue |
202|| `GET /v1/queues/{q}/jobs?state=&kind=&limit=&cursor=` | list (keyset paging) |
203|| `GET /v1/jobs/{id}`, `GET /v1/jobs/{id}/attempts`, `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/cancel`, `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/retry`, `DELETE /v1/jobs/{id}` | job verbs |
204|| `POST /v1/workers` `{name, kinds}` → `{worker_id, token}`; `DELETE /v1/workers/{id}` (releases its leases) | worker registry |
205|| `POST /v1/queues/{q}/lease` `{worker_id, max_jobs (1–100)}` → `{jobs:[{id, kind, payload, attempt, lease_token, lease_expires_at}]}` | lease a batch (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`) |
206|| `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/heartbeat` `{lease_token, extend_seconds}`; `/ack` `{lease_token, result}`; `/nack` `{lease_token, error, retry=true, delay_seconds?}` | the worker protocol |
207|| `POST /v1/schedules` `{name, queue, kind, payload, cron, timezone, enabled}`; `GET/PATCH/DELETE /v1/schedules/{id}`; `POST /v1/schedules/{id}/run` | cron schedules |
208|| `GET /v1/queues/{q}/stats`, `GET /v1/namespaces/{ns}/stats` | counts by state, oldest queued age, throughput |
209|| `GET /health`, `GET /metrics` (minimal) | ops |

211|Job states: `scheduled` (run_at in the future) → `queued` → `leased` → `succeeded` | `retry_wait` →
212|`queued` … | `dead`; `cancelled` from any non-terminal state. Events: enqueue, run_at reached,
213|lease, heartbeat, ack, nack(retry), nack(no retry), lease expired, cancel, retry, delete, purge,
214|retention sweep, worker deregistered, queue paused/resumed/deleted. The v0 code has no central
215|transition table; each handler's `UPDATE … WHERE` carries whatever guard its author remembered. That
216|is the pattern E09 names and fixes (Ch. 13.3).
217|
218|A background loop in the service, once per second: promote `scheduled` → `queued`; expire leases;
219|fire due schedules; sweep retention; ship the webhook outbox.
220|
221|**CLI** `qctl` (`queue create|ls|get|pause|resume|purge|rm`, `enqueue`, `jobs ls`, `job get|attempts|
222|cancel|retry|rm`, `worker run <q> --kinds …` (the sample worker), `schedule …`, `stats`; from E02
223|also `watch`, `job events` and `clock`). It is the explorer's main instrument (Ch. 10.1, 10.3), and
224|also its blind spot: it only ever sends well-formed requests (E03).

348|## 5. The experiment arc
349|
350|### 5.1 Shape of the history

352|```

354|explore-it/lesson-01      queuelet: experiment 01, recon of the inherited codebase (lesson 01)

356|explore-it/lesson-02      queuelet: experiment 02, make the invisible visible (lesson 02)
357|                          queuelet: close T1–T3; fix D03, D04; add checks (lesson 02)
358|explore-it/lesson-03      … experiment 03, vary the inputs and the request shape / fix D05–D08, D26 …
359|explore-it/lesson-04      … experiment 04, write the oracles down, then break them / fix D09–D11, D25, A1 …
360|explore-it/lesson-05      … experiment 05, verbs in orders nobody intended / fix D12–D14, A2 …
361|explore-it/lesson-06      … experiment 06, entities, dependents and the data's journey / fix D15–D17, A4 …
362|explore-it/lesson-07      … experiment 07, the state table and its sneak paths / fix D18–D20, A3 …
363|explore-it/lesson-08      … experiment 08, the neighbours and the clock / fix D21–D24 …
364|explore-it/lesson-09      … experiment 09, the pattern: predict the next defect, then fix the cause / fix D27 + transition table …
365|explore-it/v1-explored    explore-it: lessons index, landing page, final skills
366|```
367|
368|**Order.** Recon first (11.1, 12.4), because that is how anyone meets an inherited codebase and
369|because it produces the hypothesis backlog every later experiment draws from. Observation second
370|(Ch. 3), because its hooks are what make the later experiments possible in an hour instead of a day.
371|Then the book's own order: variations, oracles (Part I); sequences, entities, states, ecosystem
372|(Part II). Ch. 10 is practised in every experiment, since the SUT has no UI, and 10.4
373|(characterizing) is a rule of the protocol rather than a step. Last, the one Ch. 13 idea that is about
374|the code: read the findings for the pattern, predict from it, probe the prediction, fix the cause.
375|
376|**The leaner arc in one line:** *map it → make it visible → vary it → judge it → sequence it → relate
377|it → state it → surround it → explain it.* Each verb is one experiment and one probe family.
378|
379|**Tags** as above; history rewritable until Nick accepts `v1-explored`, then frozen.

381|### 5.2 The experiment protocol (`exploration/PROTOCOL.md`, written in checkpoint A)
382|
383|1. **Charter as hypothesis** (2.2, 2.3). The book's template *Explore `<target>` with `<resources>`
384|   to discover `<information>`* plus two lines the book implies and this arc makes explicit:
385|   *I predict …* (what the explorer expects, and from what: spec, code, model, or a previous
386|   surprise) and *I would be wrong if …* (what observation refutes it). One target, named
387|   instruments (tools, data, hooks, models, the spec, the source), one kind of information. The
388|   experiment's charter is written by the coordinator from this plan; the explorer may add
389|   hypotheses to the backlog, never widen the one it holds.
390|2. **Budget** (1.3). An experiment is one headless agent run with a stated budget of 60 minutes wall
391|   clock, written in the charter; the elapsed time and its split (reading / probing / writing) goes
392|   in `revealed.md`.
393|3. **Blind to the register, not to the code.** The explorer runs from an export, not a checkout:
394|   `git archive <tag> books/explore-it/project books/explore-it/exploration books/explore-it/skills
395|   books/explore-it/lessons` into an empty directory with no `.git`, no `PLAN.md`, no `register/`.
396|   Its brief names the charter, the skill to follow, the protocol, and nothing about what is
397|   planted. It reads any file in the export and runs anything in the lab. The explorer and the
398|   seeder are different model families (section 8).
399|4. **Probe log** (11.5): `notes.md`, timestamped lines tagged `#read` (something learned from the
400|   source, with `file:line`), `#obs`, `#surprise`, `#bug`, `#question`, `#hypothesis`,
401|   `#offcharter`, with the exact commands run and their output trimmed. **Revealed**
402|   (`revealed.md`): charter status (*done* / *needs more* / *blocked*); what the system showed, in
403|   plain words; the model delta (which model files changed and how); the score table (hypotheses
404|   stated / confirmed / refuted; code-reading predictions contradicted by the running system;
405|   defects found; model cells filled); the next hypotheses. An experiment may end *needs more*; it
406|   then gets a second run with a narrowed charter. An experiment closes after at most two runs;
407|   planted defects still unfound are **disclosed** in the lesson note under "What the experiment
408|   missed, and why" and fixed in the same fix commit, flagged `disclosed`.
409|5. **Follow the surprise** (10.4, 11.5, 11.6). Every `#surprise` either becomes a defect report or a
410|   written reason it is not one. A defect report (`defects/D##-<slug>.md` or `U##`): title; tag seen
411|   at; minimal steps; expected, with the **oracle named** (the Never/Always rule, the comparable
412|   system, the approximation, or the spec line); observed; variables isolated (what did not
413|   matter); the **sibling check** (where else in the code the same cause could live, with a
414|   `file:line` or "none found"); severity; status (`open` → `fixed in lesson NN` or `won't fix:
415|   <why>` or `spec`). The 11.6 procedure for a surprise that will not reproduce: record the exact
416|   state, vary one thing at a time, suspect timing and the clock, keep the log. The explorer writes
417|   the report; the coordinator reconciles it with the register (same id if planted, a `U` id if
418|   not) and the fixer writes `lab/repro/D##.sh` from the steps.
419|6. **The hypothesis backlog** (`exploration/hypotheses.md`, 2.4, 2.6): every hypothesis ever
420|   proposed, with status (`open`, `experiment NN: confirmed|refuted|needs more`), source (recon,
421|   spec silence, code reading, model cell, surprise, risk headline), and the experiment it belongs
422|   to.
423|7. **The fix** is a separate agent (the fixer, same family as the seeder) with the defect reports
424|   as its brief: the smallest patch per defect, a regression check per defect under
425|   `project/test/checks/`, the repro script, the lesson note. It does not touch anything the reports
426|   do not name. For a spec silence it also writes the spec line and records the decision in the
427|   commit body.
428|8. **Living models** (`exploration/models/`: `map.md` (entry points, packages, where each verb
429|   lands), `nouns-verbs.md`, `variables.md`, `rules.md`, `entities.md`, `states.md`,
430|   `ecosystem.md`, and from E09 `causes.md`): later experiments revise them; the diff of a model
431|   between tags is part of the story.

436|  seconds; `make down` removes everything.

438|  names, each a black-box script through `qctl`/`curl`/read-only `psql` (and the test clock) that
439|  prints `PRESENT: D18 — stale ack accepted; job 1042 succeeded with worker-a's result while worker-b

1|# 00 — The inherited system
2|
3|Queuelet is a small job queue inherited by a platform team. Producers submit JSON jobs to named queues in a namespace; workers lease them and acknowledge success or failure. Jobs can wait, retry and finish; schedules submit jobs over time. Operators manage queues and jobs. Postgres holds state, and a webhook partner records terminal notifications. An HTTP API and `qctl` are the interfaces.
4|
5|The project has source, a spec, startup instructions and tests. A passing happy path establishes a starting point; it cannot establish all the behavior you have not yet asked about. The learning artifact here is your evolving model, followed by fixes and checks for demonstrated defects.
6|
7|## Start the local system
8|
9|From the exported `books/explore-it/project/` directory:
10|
11|```sh
12|make up
13|make seed
14|make verify LESSON=00
15|```
16|
17|The baseline runner exercises enqueue → lease → ack → webhook and runs the unit and thin baseline checks. A successful run ends with `BASELINE HOLDS:` and its actual measurements. The initial live-stack run passed the unit suite and four integration checks: queue CRUD, enqueue/lease/ack/webhook, authentication, and priority with concurrent disjoint leasing. Its verdict was:
18|
19|```text
20|BASELINE HOLDS: enqueue→lease→ack→webhook; unit and happy-path checks pass
21|```
22|
23|This establishes those paths only. The baseline does not assert unprobed behavior. Use `project/README.md` for exact CLI syntax, credentials and seed manifest locations in this build. Reset fixtures with `make reset`; stop/remove the lab with `make down` when finished.
24|
25|## Read and probe in an afternoon
26|
27|Start with `project/README.md`, `project/SPEC.md` and the tests. List the promises each makes and the questions each leaves open. Follow the API entry point into handlers and persistence; trace a `qctl` command to its request and the corresponding effect. Read worker and partner-fake code as part of the system, and identify background actions alongside request handlers.
28|
29|Before executing a path, write what you think it will do and why, with a source pointer. Then run it and observe responses, command exit status, logs, database state and partner records where available. Reading supplies useful predictions; the running system can still contradict them. Keep a small map of where verbs land, then a backlog of questions ranked by consequence and uncertainty. You need not finish reading every line before making a useful probe.
30|
31|The initial exploration record is intentionally empty. Its models and hypotheses will grow from real observations. Features and hooks must be discovered in the exported build rather than assumed from a later lesson.
32|
33|## The experiment in a page
34|
35|Read [the protocol](../exploration/PROTOCOL.md). Every experiment has one target, instruments, information sought, “I predict,” “I would be wrong if,” and a 60-minute budget. The coordinator writes its charter; the explorer works within it. Read source freely inside the export and state predictions before probing.
36|
37|Keep timestamped notes with exact commands and trimmed evidence, including dead ends. Follow every surprise to a minimal reproduction or explain why it is not a defect; name the oracle that makes the result wrong. Record variables isolated and look for sibling causes. Put adjacent questions in the backlog. When the system hides an answer, request the smallest useful observation hook.
38|
39|Close with `revealed.md`: done/needs more/blocked, actual time split, observations, model delta and next hypotheses. End with the score: hypotheses stated/confirmed/refuted, code-reading predictions contradicted by execution, defects found and model cells filled. Inference is not observed coverage. At most two runs close an experiment; misses remain visible. A separate fixer turns reports into patches, reproducible checks and a lesson note. Experiment records retain their original observations.
40|
41|## Explore before reading the answers
42|
43|For a blind attempt, use a plain export of project, exploration, skills and lessons at the inherited checkpoint, without git history or the plan. The full export boundary is in the protocol. Start with [map-codebase-from-behavior](../skills/map-codebase-from-behavior/SKILL.md) and [charter-as-probe](../skills/charter-as-probe/SKILL.md). Try changing the chosen verb, its starting state, one input variable or the console you observe; write your prediction first.
44|
45|Read lessons 01–09 after your own attempt. The answer key is section 4 of the plan, outside the blind export. This lesson deliberately supplies no register, anticipated findings or filled models.
46|
47|## Where to read more
48|
49|Hendrickson, [*Explore It!*](https://pragprog.com/titles/ehxta/explore-it/) (2013), 1.1 “Two Sides of Testing,” 1.2 “Essential Elements of Exploratory Testing,” and Chapter 11 “Explore an Existing System,” especially 11.1 and 11.4. Section numbering checked against the publisher’s contents extract. This lesson is a local introduction based on the plan’s mapping; detailed source-text review remains pending. The blind-export mechanism and explicit prediction/scoring record are repo adaptations.

105|The inherited uncommitted patch was an interrupted **E01 fix**, not a new blind

110|- Worker completion now checks the current token; nack also requires leased state.
111|  Expiry records an unsuccessful attempt and dead-letters at exhaustion. Nack uses
112|  `>=` at the boundary. Retry requires dead state. These guards remain local;
113|  experiment 09 still owns the structural transition-table change.
114|- Queue deletion distinguishes missing from nonempty owners and refuses dependents.
115|  The migration also enforces ownership for new writes when deletion races an
116|  already-started enqueue/schedule request. Existing orphan rows are retained for
117|  inspection with `NOT VALID` constraints; the patch does not invent lost parents.

121|  the explorer's `limit=1000` observation did not establish a contract violation.

123|  fire on cron/zone/enable changes and clear it on disable. Firing checks enabled
124|  state, advances while paused and permits at most one catch-up execution. `Next`
125|  uses the IANA location rather than a captured fixed offset.

130|  auth-store failure returns 503 while invalid keys still return 401.

132|  queued rows. Creation timestamps retain microseconds and leasing orders ties by id.

1|# 00 — The inherited system
2|
3|Queuelet is a small job queue inherited by a platform team. Producers submit JSON jobs to named queues in a namespace; workers lease them and acknowledge success or failure. Jobs can wait, retry and finish; schedules submit jobs over time. Operators manage queues and jobs. Postgres holds state, and a webhook partner records terminal notifications. An HTTP API and `qctl` are the interfaces.
4|
5|The project has source, a spec, startup instructions and tests. A passing happy path establishes a starting point; it cannot establish all the behavior you have not yet asked about. The learning artifact here is your evolving model, followed by fixes and checks for demonstrated defects.
6|
7|## Start the local system
8|
9|From the exported `books/explore-it/project/` directory:
10|
11|```sh
12|make up
13|make seed
14|make verify LESSON=00
15|```
16|
17|The baseline runner exercises enqueue → lease → ack → webhook and runs the unit and thin baseline checks. A successful run ends with `BASELINE HOLDS:` and its actual measurements. The initial live-stack run passed the unit suite and four integration checks: queue CRUD, enqueue/lease/ack/webhook, authentication, and priority with concurrent disjoint leasing. Its verdict was:
18|
19|```text
20|BASELINE HOLDS: enqueue→lease→ack→webhook; unit and happy-path checks pass
21|```
22|
23|This establishes those paths only. The baseline does not assert unprobed behavior. Use `project/README.md` for exact CLI syntax, credentials and seed manifest locations in this build. Reset fixtures with `make reset`; stop/remove the lab with `make down` when finished.
24|
25|## Read and probe in an afternoon
26|
27|Start with `project/README.md`, `project/SPEC.md` and the tests. List the promises each makes and the questions each leaves open. Follow the API entry point into handlers and persistence; trace a `qctl` command to its request and the corresponding effect. Read worker and partner-fake code as part of the system, and identify background actions alongside request handlers.
28|
29|Before executing a path, write what you think it will do and why, with a source pointer. Then run it and observe responses, command exit status, logs, database state and partner records where available. Reading supplies useful predictions; the running system can still contradict them. Keep a small map of where verbs land, then a backlog of questions ranked by consequence and uncertainty. You need not finish reading every line before making a useful probe.
30|
31|The initial exploration record is intentionally empty. Its models and hypotheses will grow from real observations. Features and hooks must be discovered in the exported build rather than assumed from a later lesson.
32|
33|## The experiment in a page
34|
35|Read [the protocol](../exploration/PROTOCOL.md). Every experiment has one target, instruments, information sought, “I predict,” “I would be wrong if,” and a 60-minute budget. The coordinator writes its charter; the explorer works within it. Read source freely inside the export and state predictions before probing.
36|
37|Keep timestamped notes with exact commands and trimmed evidence, including dead ends. Follow every surprise to a minimal reproduction or explain why it is not a defect; name the oracle that makes the result wrong. Record variables isolated and look for sibling causes. Put adjacent questions in the backlog. When the system hides an answer, request the smallest useful observation hook.
38|
39|Close with `revealed.md`: done/needs more/blocked, actual time split, observations, model delta and next hypotheses. End with the score: hypotheses stated/confirmed/refuted, code-reading predictions contradicted by execution, defects found and model cells filled. Inference is not observed coverage. At most two runs close an experiment; misses remain visible. A separate fixer turns reports into patches, reproducible checks and a lesson note. Experiment records retain their original observations.
40|
41|## Explore before reading the answers
42|
43|For a blind attempt, use a plain export of project, exploration, skills and lessons at the inherited checkpoint, without git history or the plan. The full export boundary is in the protocol. Start with [map-codebase-from-behavior](../skills/map-codebase-from-behavior/SKILL.md) and [charter-as-probe](../skills/charter-as-probe/SKILL.md). Try changing the chosen verb, its starting state, one input variable or the console you observe; write your prediction first.
44|
45|Read lessons 01–09 after your own attempt. The answer key is section 4 of the plan, outside the blind export. This lesson deliberately supplies no register, anticipated findings or filled models.
46|
47|## Where to read more
48|
49|Hendrickson, [*Explore It!*](https://pragprog.com/titles/ehxta/explore-it/) (2013), 1.1 “Two Sides of Testing,” 1.2 “Essential Elements of Exploratory Testing,” and Chapter 11 “Explore an Existing System,” especially 11.1 and 11.4. Section numbering checked against the publisher’s contents extract. This lesson is a local introduction based on the plan’s mapping; detailed source-text review remains pending. The blind-export mechanism and explicit prediction/scoring record are repo adaptations.

# F01 — Ack completes a leased job without checking the lease token

- Seen at: `explore-it/v0-inherited` (blind export); isolated stack `queuelet-e01`, image `queuelet:e01` built from the export 2026-10-22T01:39–01:40Z. Fixture: `lab/reset.sh` seed at 01:41:03Z.
- Original observation: [notes.md](../experiments/01-map-it/notes.md) H02, entries 01:41:54Z–01:41:55Z.

## Minimal reproduction
Actor acme-key; any queue; worker registered with kind `echo`.
1. `POST /v1/queues/h02/jobs {"kind":"echo","payload":{"a":1}}` → 201 id 302.
2. `POST /v1/queues/h02/lease {"worker_id":4,"max_jobs":1}` → job 302 leased with token `75de57db…`.
3. `POST /v1/jobs/302/ack {"lease_token":"not-the-token","result":{"by":"impostor"}}`.

## Expected (oracle)
SPEC.md, Worker protocol: "Only the current lease holder may complete or extend a job." → 409 `state_conflict`, job stays `leased`.

## Observed
```
{"ok":true} [HTTP 200]
302|succeeded|1|{"by": "impostor"}
```
The real holder's later ack would get 409; the impostor's result is stored and notified.

## Variables isolated
- Token value: any string (here `not-the-token`). Job must be in state `leased` (ack.go filter); state did matter for ack, unlike nack (F02).
- Did not matter: payload, queue config.
- Control: heartbeat with a wrong token → 409 (H31, 01:46:19Z), so the token check exists for heartbeat only.

## Sibling check
Predicted before probing H03/H27/H31: nack (internal/jobs/nack.go:10) has no token filter → confirmed, see F02. heartbeat (internal/jobs/jobs.go:91) filters token → probe H31 confirmed it rejects. Lease release on worker delete (internal/api/jobs.go:110) is by worker id, not token — by design.

## Severity / status
High: any caller in the namespace (or with F03, any namespace) can complete another worker's job with a forged result; double-execution protection rests on the token. Status: open.

# Map codebase from behavior

Draft for execution against queuelet. In this arc follow [the protocol](../../exploration/PROTOCOL.md); operate within the export and assigned charter.

## When to use

Inheriting a service, finding its entry points, or asking how it actually works.

## Inputs

A runnable local system, source, startup instructions, spec, tests, exploration record and time budget.

## Procedure

1. Set a recon boundary and budget. Read startup instructions, spec and test entry points; distinguish documented promises, assumptions and behavior demonstrated by existing checks.
2. Trace entry points into packages, persistence and background work. Record each noun and verb, its handler and source pointers in map.md and nouns-verbs.md. A source pointer predicts a path; it does not prove the path executes.
3. Predict a representative end-to-end path before running it, then walk documented verbs within the budget. Retain commands, responses, exit status and persistent effects beside source-based predictions.
4. Read spec sentences for silences and ways they could be false. Find where code decides the missing behavior. Write each prediction, its source and refutation condition before probing.
5. Rank remaining hypotheses by consequence and uncertainty. Name a fitting probe family: variation, oracle, sequence/state, entity/data journey or ecosystem/boundary. Backlog off-charter questions.
6. Keep models proportional to evidence: start with map and nouns/verbs, then add variables, rules, entities, states and ecosystem. Mark inferred and unprobed cells. Once findings exist, group causes and predict a sibling location before probing it.

## Output

A source-and-behavior map, nouns/verbs list and ranked hypothesis backlog with source, prediction, refutation condition, probe family, status and evidence links.

## Source

Elisabeth Hendrickson, [*Explore It!*](https://pragprog.com/titles/ehxta/explore-it/) (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2013), sections 11.1, 11.4, 12.4, 2.4, 2.6 and 13.3. Section numbering checked against the publisher’s contents extract. This draft adapts the approved plan’s chapter map; detailed source-text review is pending. The procedure and local record formats are repo guidance, not quotations from the book.

## Worked example

Pending real experiments. E01 will supply the recon and initial models; E09 the causal map. A second run against litefleet’s tenant API awaits both arcs. No run results or scores are claimed yet.

  IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns
             WHERE table_name='jobs' AND column_name='created_at'
               AND data_type='timestamp without time zone') THEN
    ALTER TABLE jobs ALTER COLUMN created_at TYPE timestamptz(6)
      USING created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC';
  END IF;
  -- Existing orphan rows are retained for inspection; new writes/deletes must
  -- preserve ownership even when enqueue and owner deletion race.
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname='jobs_queue_owner') THEN
    ALTER TABLE jobs ADD CONSTRAINT jobs_queue_owner
      FOREIGN KEY (queue_id) REFERENCES queues(id) NOT VALID;
  END IF;
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname='schedules_queue_owner') THEN
    ALTER TABLE schedules ADD CONSTRAINT schedules_queue_owner
      FOREIGN KEY (queue_id) REFERENCES queues(id) NOT VALID;
  END IF;
END $$;

# F01 — Ack completes a leased job without checking the lease token

- Seen at: `explore-it/v0-inherited` (blind export); isolated stack `queuelet-e01`, image `queuelet:e01` built from the export 2026-10-22T01:39–01:40Z. Fixture: `lab/reset.sh` seed at 01:41:03Z.
- Original observation: [notes.md](../experiments/01-map-it/notes.md) H02, entries 01:41:54Z–01:41:55Z.

## Minimal reproduction
Actor acme-key; any queue; worker registered with kind `echo`.
1. `POST /v1/queues/h02/jobs {"kind":"echo","payload":{"a":1}}` → 201 id 302.
2. `POST /v1/queues/h02/lease {"worker_id":4,"max_jobs":1}` → job 302 leased with token `75de57db…`.
3. `POST /v1/jobs/302/ack {"lease_token":"not-the-token","result":{"by":"impostor"}}`.

## Expected (oracle)
SPEC.md, Worker protocol: "Only the current lease holder may complete or extend a job." → 409 `state_conflict`, job stays `leased`.

## Observed
```
{"ok":true} [HTTP 200]
302|succeeded|1|{"by": "impostor"}
```
The real holder's later ack would get 409; the impostor's result is stored and notified.

## Variables isolated
- Token value: any string (here `not-the-token`). Job must be in state `leased` (ack.go filter); state did matter for ack, unlike nack (F02).
- Did not matter: payload, queue config.
- Control: heartbeat with a wrong token → 409 (H31, 01:46:19Z), so the token check exists for heartbeat only.

## Sibling check
Predicted before probing H03/H27/H31: nack (internal/jobs/nack.go:10) has no token filter → confirmed, see F02. heartbeat (internal/jobs/jobs.go:91) filters token → probe H31 confirmed it rejects. Lease release on worker delete (internal/api/jobs.go:110) is by worker id, not token — by design.

## Severity / status
High: any caller in the namespace (or with F03, any namespace) can complete another worker's job with a forged result; double-execution protection rests on the token. Status: open.

# Map codebase from behavior

Draft for execution against queuelet. In this arc follow [the protocol](../../exploration/PROTOCOL.md); operate within the export and assigned charter.

## When to use

Inheriting a service, finding its entry points, or asking how it actually works.

## Inputs

A runnable local system, source, startup instructions, spec, tests, exploration record and time budget.

## Procedure

1. Set a recon boundary and budget. Read startup instructions, spec and test entry points; distinguish documented promises, assumptions and behavior demonstrated by existing checks.
2. Trace entry points into packages, persistence and background work. Record each noun and verb, its handler and source pointers in map.md and nouns-verbs.md. A source pointer predicts a path; it does not prove the path executes.
3. Predict a representative end-to-end path before running it, then walk documented verbs within the budget. Retain commands, responses, exit status and persistent effects beside source-based predictions.
4. Read spec sentences for silences and ways they could be false. Find where code decides the missing behavior. Write each prediction, its source and refutation condition before probing.
5. Rank remaining hypotheses by consequence and uncertainty. Name a fitting probe family: variation, oracle, sequence/state, entity/data journey or ecosystem/boundary. Backlog off-charter questions.
6. Keep models proportional to evidence: start with map and nouns/verbs, then add variables, rules, entities, states and ecosystem. Mark inferred and unprobed cells. Once findings exist, group causes and predict a sibling location before probing it.

## Output

A source-and-behavior map, nouns/verbs list and ranked hypothesis backlog with source, prediction, refutation condition, probe family, status and evidence links.

## Source

Elisabeth Hendrickson, [*Explore It!*](https://pragprog.com/titles/ehxta/explore-it/) (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2013), sections 11.1, 11.4, 12.4, 2.4, 2.6 and 13.3. The procedure and local record formats are repo guidance, not quotations from the book.

## Worked example
